To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the age-specific physiological parameters and the high efficiency and maturation of carboxylesterases (CESs) in children result in comparable to or lower internal exposure in brain in children than in adults in response of the same level of pyrethroid exposure (Cmax ratio between 1- to 25-year old is 0.69-0.94 for the 8 pyrethyroids studied).
a life stage PBPK model, coupled with IVIV, provides a robust approach for evaluating age-related sensitivity to a class of chemicals.

1) a life-stage PBTK modeling approach coupled with IVIVE provides a robust framework to evaluate the age-related differences in internal dose of the pyrethyroid class of chemicals; and 2) the high efficiency and maturation of CES enzymes result in very efficient metabolic clearance of these chemicals across ages, leading in most cases to a lower internal dose in children than that of adults.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of a PBPK model to the assessment of internal dose of pyrethroid insecticides.
understanding how pyrethroids are metabolized in children, and the implications for their toxicity.
the age-related differences in the pharmacokinetics and target tissue (brain, blood) exposure of pyrethroid insecticides in humans.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are no age-related differences in internal exposure of pyrethroid pesticides in the brain.
, based on the current understanding and available data, the differences in the internal dose of pyrethroid insecticides in the brain between children and adults are not expected to be large.
the age-related sensitivity of children to pyrethroid pesticides is unlikely due to differences in internal dose.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for all pyrethroids evaluated, the internal dose in the target tissue in children is lower or comparable to that in adults in the same exposure scenario.
the PBPK modeling results indicate that the age-related differences in target tissue (brain or blood) exposure to pyrethroid pesticides are small.

the efficient hepatic clearance of pyrethrins across ages and the blood flow-limited hepatic metabolism of pyrethrines result in comparable or even lower internal exposures in the target tissue in children than that of adults in response to a given pythroid exposure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for the pyrethed class of chemicals, there is no evidence for age-related sensitivity in humans, and the use of a PBPK model to evaluate internal dose is a valuable tool to assess this.

the high metabolic efficiency in children, coupled with the rapid maturation of the liver, results in a low internal target tissue exposure to pyrethroid pesticides in children compared to adults, and that this should be considered when evaluating the potential for developmental and reproductive toxicity.

, except for a few pyrethroids such as bifenthrin and trans-permethrin for which the contribution of P450 enzymes is more important, CES enzymes are responsible for the majority of the hepatic metabolism of pyrethroid pesticides.
